transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-30
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~46 minutes
Attendees: Samira Khan (Redwood AE), Evan Li (Redwood SE), Priya Desai (Redwood SE), Mark Reynolds (CTO, Lacuna), Aisha Patel (Lead ML Eng, Lacuna), Jordan Mills (Platform Ops, Lacuna), Sofia Chen (Security, Lacuna)

Summary (auto): quick discovery on reliability requirements, multi-region fallback needs, SLA expectations; discussed Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs and next steps for POC benchmarks and security docs.

Transcript:
[00:00] Samira Khan: All right, thanks everyone for joining, I'm Samira from Redwood, I'm the AE on this. Evan and Priya are with me from solutions and we'll mostly be listening for the technical bits. Mark, Aisha, Jordan, Sofia, thanks for carving out time. Can you give a quick context about Lacuna's use cases and reliability concerns?
[00:18] Mark Reynolds: Yeah thanks Samira. So we run patient intake and triage workflows, critical during peak hours. The main ask is near real-time responses, our internal SLA is 200ms p95 for inference in the happy path but we can accept up to 800ms during degradation. We're evaluating whether Redwood Hosted can fit or whether we need Dedicated or Private for more control.
[00:38] Aisha Patel: To add — we have about 150 qps average, spikes to 500 qps during campaigns. State is sensitive PHI-ish, so encryption at rest and in transit plus audit logs are musts. We also need multi-region failover because we serve East US and EU.
[00:55] Evan Li: Got it. Thanks. Just to confirm, the 200ms p95 — is that per token or end-to-end turn?
[01:03] Aisha Patel: End-to-end for short prompts, like < 128 tokens. Most calls are single-turn.
[01:08] Priya Desai: Ok. Quick note on mis-voice: we sometimes see the transcription say K-V cache as K-V cash, ignore that.
[01:15] Jordan Mills: Also, procurement side — we need predictable pricing for capacity planning. Bursty traffic is a concern.
[01:22] Samira Khan: Totally. High level, Redwood offers Hosted (fast onboarding), Dedicated (reserved GPU pools), and Private (VPC / on-prem) — each has different tradeoffs for control, SLAs, and routing. For reliability: we have multi-region routing, model variant fallbacks, and automated capacity tier fallbacks. But let's dig into specifics for your constraints.
[01:38] Mark Reynolds: Boundary conditions — if a region degrades, what's the failover time? And how do you ensure consistency for sessions that have KV cache warm? We can't just route to a cold instance and lose context for conversational flows.
[01:50] Evan Li: Great question. For Dedicated and Private, we can replicate KV cache across regions asynchronously for warm standby. In Hosted we rely more on prefix/KV caching per-pop and fast cold starts with optimized kernels; we also support read-through cache and sticky routing to keep low latency. Failover time depends on detection and routing policy but typically you'll see detection plus reroute in 10s to low minutes; warm standby reduces the effective cold penalty.
[02:18] Aisha Patel: 10s to minutes is quite a range. For us, 30s is borderline for patient flows. How deterministic is the 10s number?
[02:26] Evan Li: It's not a hard SLA for Hosted; that's why larger customers use Dedicated with cross-region replication and explicit healthchecks to meet tight RTOs. With Dedicated multi-region pools and active-active routing plus KV replication, we've seen typical failover under 15s in our benchmarks, though that depends on model size and KV synchronization window.
[02:44] Sofia Chen: From security: if you replicate state cross-region, how's encryption handled? Do you support customer-managed keys? And are audit logs preserved across failover?
[02:53] Priya Desai: Yes, we integrate with KMS/HSM for customer-managed keys on Dedicated and Private. Audit logs are streamed to the customer's SIEM and we maintain continuity across failovers; there's a short window for transfer but events are timestamped and ordered. We'll share the docs.
[03:09] Jordan Mills: For cost: if we do active-active in two regions, that doubles reserved capacity, right? How do you optimize?
[03:17] Evan Li: Active-active does mean more reserved capacity; we provide burst and fractional allocation strategies — e.g., a hot primary and warm standby with autoscale policies and fast warmup. Redwood Optimize can recommend batching and quantization to reduce per-token cost. There are also routing policies to send non-latency-critical traffic to cheaper regions.
[03:34] Mark Reynolds: Another thing — we have regulatory requirements that certain records remain in-region for EU users. How do multi-region fallbacks respect data residency?
[03:43] Samira Khan: Good point. Our routing policies support geo-aware routing and can be configured to avoid cross-border fallback for regulated traffic. For those sessions we would have stricter fallbacks (e.g., degrade model fidelity instead of routing out-of-region). We can document the options.
[03:58] Aisha Patel: Ok that's promising. Could you explain fallback policies in more detail—like model variant fallback vs region fallback vs degraded latency mode?
[04:07] Evan Li: Sure. There are three common patterns: 1) Model variant fallback — route to a smaller quantized variant of the same model when capacity is constrained; this reduces latency and cost but may slightly change output quality. 2) Region fallback — route to another region's pool; used if primary region is down. 3) Graceful degradation — change runtime config (lower max tokens, reduce sampling work, larger batching) to keep latency SLAs. You can chain these with policies: prefer variant fallback first, then warm standby region, then degraded mode.
[04:38] Mark Reynolds: For variant fallbacks, how do you measure quality delta? We need to ensure triage decisions don't materially change.
[04:45] Evan Li: We use eval suites and baseline prompts; Redwood Optimize provides per-prompt regression alerts and can tie quality metrics to rollouts. For POC we can run side-by-side comparisons on your traffic to quantify drift.
[04:56] Aisha Patel: Great. Can you commit to SLAs for Dedicated? We need uptime guarantees and credits if you miss them.
[05:03] Samira Khan: Dedicated comes with SLA-backed uptime and latency targets under contract. We usually include credits for downtime and a defined remediation plan. The exact numbers depend on committed capacity and contract terms; we can propose an SLA aligned to your risk tolerance.
[05:15] Jordan Mills: If we start with Hosted for speed, can we migrate to Dedicated without significant integration changes?
[05:22] Priya Desai: Yes — the API and config layer is consistent. Migration steps are mostly infra and provisioning. We'll help with pinning model versions and rollout policies. Many customers do a Hosted-to-Dedicated ramp after proofs.
[05:33] Mark Reynolds: What about troubleshooting — do you provide tracing hooks we can integrate into our observability?
[05:38] Evan Li: Redwood Console exposes per-request tracing, token-level latency breakdowns, and can stream traces to your tracing backend. We also provide alerting for error rates and fallback triggers.
[05:49] Sofia Chen: On SOC 2 and pen tests — will you share compliance docs and can you do an on-site review if needed?
[05:55] Samira Khan: We'll share SOC 2 and our security whitepaper. For Private deployments we can support more stringent reviews; for Dedicated we have enterprise processes — we can discuss NDA and next steps after this call.
[06:05] Mark Reynolds: Timeline question — we want to be beta-ready by end of Q1 2027. Is that realistic?
[06:11] Samira Khan: Yep, that's achievable. Typically POC and benchmarking take 2–4 weeks, then provisioning for Dedicated might take additional 4–6 weeks depending on capacity ordering. If you sign early we can prioritize.
[06:22] Aisha Patel: For the benchmarking POC, we need Redwood to run perf tests with our sample workload and also a cold-start storm test.
[06:29] Evan Li: We'll design a perf test plan: steady-state p95, peak p99, cold-start storm, and failover scenarios. We can run that on Hosted first, then repeat on Dedicated.
[06:38] Jordan Mills: Can you do a price estimate for a Dedicated active-active two-region config with 8 gpus per region?
[06:44] Samira Khan: We'll send a tailored estimate. Quick back-of-envelope: pricing depends on GPU type, reserved terms, and expected utilization; we'll include cost for KMS and extended retention if you need it.
[06:55] Priya Desai: Quick note about transcription — some proper nouns may be off in the transcript, e.g., KV cache spelled weird, and our product name sometimes transcribed as Redwood inference as two words.
[07:03] Mark Reynolds: Understood.
[07:06] Samira Khan: Ok let's recap real quick. Action items: Samira will send Dedicated pricing and SOC2/security docs; Evan to share fallback architecture and perf plan; Aisha to share traffic profile and SLA targets. We schedule the POC week of 12/7 — does that work?
[07:20] Aisha Patel: Yes that week works for us.
[07:24] Jordan Mills: One last question — in failure scenarios, do you support per-tenant fallback policies? We want different products to have different tolerances.
[07:32] Evan Li: Yes, per-tenant routing and policy overrides are supported so you can set stricter flows for regulated products and more aggressive fallbacks for non-critical ones.
[07:41] Samira Khan: Great. We'll follow up with the materials and propose a POC schedule. Thanks everyone.
[07:47] Mark Reynolds: Thanks all.

End of transcript. Shared artifacts mentioned: link to pricing spreadsheet (https://redwood.example.com/poc-pricing-lacuna), link to security pack (https://redwood.example.com/security/soc2-redwood.pdf), perf plan template (https://redwood.example.com/templates/perf-plan.pdf).
